text:
Am I crazy to want to leave tech?

I feel like everything I loved about the job is gone. I’m an engineer with a bit over 2 years full time experience, making ~140k at a really comfortable and easy job. My manager, culture, and teammates are all great. The work is easy (thanks to Claude), but I have lost all joy for it. 
 Because of AI, I literally do not have to do anything anymore except: prompt, read, prompt, repeat. Some days, I don’t do more than 10 minutes of work. The satisfaction I got (not even that long ago) from writing something, testing it, and seeing it work has disappeared. The AI can do it 10x as fast (and now as well) as me. I’m starting to feel like my value as an engineer and as a human being is fading. Also, there’s no way my mental ability is staying intact. If AI disappears tomorrow I’d have no clue how to do my job.
 I’m thinking of switching to something more real: EMS, policing, fire. Something where I don’t have to interact with AI and where my work doesn’t feel meaningless. Also, I’ve always loved interacting with people and genuinely despise sitting at a desk and working silently. 
 I told my (immigrant) parents about this and they are extremely upset with me. They say I should just stick it out and continue. For them, doing something “smart” matters more than happiness. In my opinion, being smart won’t be the advantage it used to be in 5 years. 
 What do you think? 
 Note: I also have over $320k saved because I knew when I started working in tech that I wouldn’t want to do it forever, I just didn’t know it would be this quick.

Why am I working more if AI was supposed to make coding easier?

I have over nine years of experience in ML and have always worked hard to keep up with the industry, but for the past year and a half, I’ve been working to the point of burnout.
 Over the last year or so i am and most of my friends and colleagues are working 10–12 hours a day, six days a week as companies have shifted to being "AI-first" or "AI-native," it is absolutely contrary to the claim that AI would make developers' lives easier and cut down on work time—the exact opposite is happening. 
 This is happening partly because we constantly have to learn new AI-related development tools, and partly because management pressures us to speed things up. Of course, no one can say no; we’ve already been through one round of layoffs and are expecting another—and I don’t need to tell you how hard it is to find a job right now. So, people are desperately clinging to their jobs and grinding away late into the night, terrified of falling behind the market or underperforming and getting fired.
 Ultimately I has a feeling this productivity boost has less to do with AI but more with a overtime. Is it like this for everyone, or did I just get unlucky?

text:
2 years into my software engineering career and AI is making me feel lost about my career

I'm a software engineer with around 2 years of professional experience, and lately I've been feeling pretty lost about my career because of AI.
 I started learning backend development before AI became such a big part of software development. I used to spend a lot of time reading documentation, Stack Overflow, existing code, debugging things myself, etc. When I started my first job, I had a lot of ownership over a backend project and learned a ton because I had to figure things out myself. I was genuinely passionate about programming.
 A few months ago I joined a much larger company hoping I'd learn how large-scale systems are built and have more experienced engineers around me. Instead, I haven't really learned much, and I've become heavily dependent on AI & Cursor over the past 6 months.
 My productivity has definitely increased, but I feel like I'm losing the part of development that actually made me learn. I used to review everything AI generated and make sure I understood it. Now the codebases are large enough that it's becoming difficult to fully understand everything AI does, so I often end up trusting its understanding of the codebase.
 That's what worries me. I'm only 2 years into my career and I feel like I should be building my engineering fundamentals, not becoming dependent on a tool that understands the codebase better than I do.
 I brought this up with my manager and he basically told me to use AI to learn instead of relying on other people mentoring you. Maybe he's right, but I don't really know how to do that effectively.
 So I'd like to hear from more experienced engineers:
  How do you use AI without letting it replace the thinking/learning part of engineering?
 If you were 2 years into your career today, what would you focus on learning?
 Do you think less experienced engineers should approach learning differently in the AI era?
  TL;DR: AI has made me much faster at work, but after 6 months of heavily relying on Cursor, I feel like I'm learning less and becoming dependent on it. I'm worried about becoming good at shipping code without actually becoming a better engineer. How should I approach learning and using AI at this stage of my career?

text:
More tech unionization - 1,900 Blizzard Developers Just Won A Union Contract Full Of Protections For AI, Layoffs, And More

https://kotaku.com/blizzard-workers-union-contract-microsoft-2000732422
 Not quite impossible for tech to shape up 
 Blizz devs just unionized and got:
 - Any implementation of AI technology that materially impacts union-performed work must be bargained over before Microsoft can roll it out.
 - Staff get two months of advance layoff warning, guaranteed severance payouts, and over a year of priority re-hiring rights if cuts occur.
 - Remote work is no longer subject to sudden executive whim or opaque denials.
 - Leaving the studio or getting laid off before launch will no longer erase a developer from the final credits
 - future corporate takeover cannot nullify these terms.
 So the learned helplessness about tech unions was wrong. Doesn’t stop a layoff but makes it a lot softer

text:
Can I leverage a job I just started to negotiate another offer?

I recently started a new job at Company A and looking for some advice on how to handle another offer.
 I applied to Company B before starting at Company A. The process with B continued afterward, I completed the loop, and recently received a verbal offer.
 Originally B was considering me for the same level I’m currently at at A. I asked to be evaluated for the next level based on the scope/level I had at my previous company, went through the additional process, and got the up-level.
 Comp-wise, B is roughly in line with A overall. B has a higher base and better long-term compensation, but year 1 is slightly lower because A gave me a very large sign-on bonus. B would also require relocation.
 The complication is that throughout the interview process, Company B was under the impression I was still at my previous employer. My recent move to Company A never came up, and nobody directly asked about my current employment situation, so I never mentioned it. Most of the interviews were centered around experience from my previous company.
 During the verbal offer conversation, the recruiter said there isn’t much room to increase the offer unless I can provide documentation supporting higher current compensation or another competing package.
 I mentioned that my current compensation is around X, and the recruiter asked me to provide documentation. A significant portion of that compensation is the sign-on bonus from Company A that I’d be giving up by leaving so soon.
 My questions are:
 Is it reasonable to use the offer letter from Company A as documentation of my current compensation, even though I already accepted it and have only been there about a month?
 Since Company B didn’t know I had already moved to Company A, does bringing this up now look shady or create a risk of the verbal offer being rescinded?
 If you were in this situation, how would you explain the change to the recruiter before providing the documentation? Would you even do it at all? 
 TLDR: I started Company A about a month ago while Company B’s interview process was already underway. B never knew I had switched jobs and thought I was still at my previous company. I now have a verbal offer from B, but it’s slightly below my current comp because I’d be giving up a large sign-on at A. Recruiter said comp won’t change without documentation of higher current pay. Can I use my accepted Company A offer/current comp as leverage, and does revealing the job change now risk looking shady or getting the offer pulled?

text:
My job is making me question my abilities as a dev

Hey everyone, I wanted to vent a little and get some outside perspectives on my current work situation.
 TL;DR:
 Dev with 5yoe, got moved to a new project just over a week ago with almost no onboarding. My manager thinks I'm underperforming and lacking autonomy, expecting me to find bugs, implement improvements, build dashboards, and deliver constantly. It's making me question my abilities and feel burned out.
 Is this normal for a mid-level dev? How do you guys handle unfamiliar codebases? Should I try to improve my situation or start looking for another job?
 Wall of text here:
 I have around 5 years of experience as a developer and work at a fairly big company in my country. A little over a week ago, I was moved to a different team and project due to an internal reorganization.
 My onboarding basically consisted of: "Clone this repo. It's yours now. Find bugs, fix them, and implement improvements." Since then, I've been analyzing the codebase using Codex, trying to understand how everything works.
 Recently, my manager criticized my performance, saying I'm taking too long, lack autonomy, and that my performance is closer to a junior developer's than a mid-level's. He expects me to already be generating bug reports, fixing issues, building dashboards, and proactively identifying improvements.
 I explained that I'm still getting familiar with the system and that parallelizing all these tasks after barely a week on the project is challenging.
 We're also heavily encouraged to use AI for practically everything, which has been burning me out. I feel like there's more emphasis on producing output quickly than actually understanding what we're building.
 What bothers me most is that I've never had my abilities questioned like this before. In previous jobs, I've built features end to end, deployed to production, worked with stakeholders, discussed about technical solutions with peers/leaders and handled tasks independently. I don't think I lack autonomy, I mean that I've never felt like I needed someone constantly holding my hand to get things done besides asking some questions to my manager/ seniors. I usually come with a solution and asks if its okay, i dont like going without anything and expect to get everything solved. but I do need some time to understand a project before I can confidently suggest improvements.
 Now I feel like nothing I do is enough, and it's honestly making me question my abilities as a developer.
 I'm also curious about how you approach unfamiliar codebases
 my usual workflow is to explain the task and context to AI, propose an approach, and iterate on its suggestions until I fully understand and agree with the solution. Sometimes I wonder if I'm spending too much time trying to understand things instead of just implementing them.
 So, a few questions:
 Are these reasonable expectations for a mid level developer after just one week?
 How do you approach understanding an unfamiliar codebase with AI? Am I being inefficient?
 Would you try to turn this situation around or start looking for another job?
 For context, I have 5 years of experience, mainly with React, Node.js, TypeScript, and .NET. I'm considering looking elsewhere, but I'm unsure how difficult finding another job would be in the current market.
